resources.title: American black duck
resources.description: Identify American black duck, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: American black duck (Anas rubripes) can be identified as follows: Large dark dabbling duck with a pale head, dark body and violet-blue speculum; females and hybrids can resemble female Mallards. This biological profile does not establish whether hunting or trapping is legal.

identification.text: Large dark dabbling duck with a pale head, dark body and violet-blue speculum; females and hybrids can resemble female Mallards.

habitat.text: Eastern wooded wetlands, salt marshes and coastal estuaries.

resources.title: Wood duck
resources.description: Identify Wood duck, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Wood duck (Aix sponsa) can be identified as follows: Compact crested duck; males are multicoloured with bold white facial lines, females gray-brown with a distinct white eye patch. This biological profile does not establish whether hunting or trapping is legal.

identification.text: Compact crested duck; males are multicoloured with bold white facial lines, females gray-brown with a distinct white eye patch.

habitat.text: Wooded swamps, beaver ponds and tree-lined wetlands.

resources.title: Northern pintail

resources.quickAnswer: Northern pintail (Anas acuta) can be identified as follows: Long-necked, slender duck with a pointed tail; males have a chocolate head and white neck stripe, females are finely patterned brown. This biological profile does not establish whether hunting or trapping is legal.

identification.text: Long-necked, slender duck with a pointed tail; males have a chocolate head and white neck stripe, females are finely patterned brown.

habitat.text: Shallow open wetlands, prairie potholes, marshes and coastal flats.

resources.title: Gadwall
resources.description: Identify Gadwall, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Gadwall (Mareca strepera) can be identified as follows: Subtle gray-brown dabbling duck with a white wing patch; males have fine vermiculation and a black rear, females resemble female Mallards but show white in the wing. This biological profile does not establish whether hunting or trapping is legal.

resources.quickAnswer: Lesser scaup (Aythya affinis) can be identified as follows: Medium diving duck with a peaked rear crown; males often show a purplish head sheen, but structure and habitat are more useful than sheen alone. resources.quickAnswer: Common goldeneye (Bucephala clangula) can be identified as follows: Compact diving duck with a large angular head; males have a round white spot before the golden eye, females have a brown head. This biological profile does not establish whether hunting or trapping is legal.

resources.description: Identify Barrow's goldeneye, compare important lookalikes, and understand its North American range without inferring legal hunting status.
resources.quickAnswer: Barrow's goldeneye (Bucephala islandica) can be identified as follows: Males have a crescent-shaped white face patch and black shoulder marks; females are best separated from common goldeneye with multiple traits. This biological profile does not establish whether hunting or trapping is legal.

resources.quickAnswer: Snow goose (Anser caerulescens) can be identified as follows: White morph is mostly white with black wingtips; blue morph has a dark body and white head. Both have a pink bill with a dark grin patch. This biological profile does not establish whether hunting or trapping is legal.

This biological profile does not establish whether hunting or trapping is legal.
